newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Big trades in S&P 500 index.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS/Big trades in S&P 500 index.

text.p: Trading in S&P 500 index options took the spotlight Thursday as some big trades crossed, mostly on the put side.
The most dramatic was in the October 655 call, where 20,575 contracts changed hands by 1430 CDT (1930 GMT). The option's open interest was about 25,700 contracts.
The majority of the volume was crossed in three major blocks of 8,000, 6,570 and 6,000.
"It was all done as a spread," said Michael Schwartz, managing director at Oppenheimer & Co.
The SPX spot index was down 1.90 at 692.11 and had traded between 691.84 and 694.81.
About 10,135 contracts in the SPX October 675 put traded and Schwartz said some of that volume, also mainly spreads, could be related to the action in the October 655 puts.
He said an investor could have done a two-for-one ratio spread in the October 655s and 675s.
"They were probably trying to put on an inexpensive hedge by doing the ratio where they were selling probably an even-money spread," Schwartz said.
"It could be an inexpensive even-money correction hedge," he said, explaining that that strategy would not cost the investor much even if the market does not correct its recent rally.
Heavy trading was also seen in several November SPX options.
The November 695 put traded 6,725 contracts, the November 635 put traded 6,500, the November 725 call traded just over 6,000 and the November 680 put traded nearly 6,000.
Schwartz said much of the volume in those options was also spreads and could have been linked.
"It's all probably part of the same FOB - Friend of Bill or Friend of Bob - position," he said.

He explained that the positions could have been taken by an investor interested in hedging for a market reaction to the November 5 U.S. presidential election that pits Democrat President Bill Clinton against Republican challenger Bob Dole.
"That's understandable because (the election) may be as good an excuse as any to start the long anticipated correction," Schwartz added.
November options expire on November 16. -Gregory Crawford, 312-408-8750/E-mail: derivatives@reuters.com
